draft.title: Colons and brackets
card: A colon (:) introduces a list, an example or an explanation. It comes after a complete main clause, such as "We need three things:" before the list.
A colon can also lead into an explanation. "Sam was happy: his team had won." The words after the colon explain the first part.
Brackets ( ) hold extra information. "The museum (built in 1890) is near the station."
Take out the brackets and the words inside them, and the sentence must still make sense: "The museum is near the station."
draft.remember: A colon introduces what follows. Brackets hold extra information that can be removed.

opts: Our school (founded in 1950) has a big oval
Our school (has a big) oval founded in 1950
Our (school founded in) 1950 has a big oval
Our school has a (big oval founded in 1950
a.why: The words inside the brackets are extra, and the sentence still works without them. In the other options, removing the bracketed words leaves a broken sentence.
a.clue: Cross out the bracketed words and reread.

b.q: Zara packed three snacks an apple, a muesli bar and some grapes. Where does the colon belong?
opts: After snacks
After packed
After three
After apple
b.why: A colon goes after the complete main clause "Zara packed three snacks", to introduce the list. Putting it after apple would split the list.
b.clue: The colon comes before the list starts.

a.best: Our school (founded in 1950) has a big oval

problems.detail: Why (a) says removing the bracketed words breaks the other sentences. But 'Our school has a (big oval founded in 1950' has no closing bracket, so its real fault is the unclosed bracket. The why should name this.
